title: Modules courbes elliptiques en caractéristiques ≠2 : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting. E is an elliptic curve over a field k with char k ≠ 2, with origin 0. F_n = Γ(E, O(n·0)) is the space of functions with a pole of order at most n at 0. F_n^± are the eigenspaces of the involution [-1]. J = E[2] \ {0} is the set of three nontrivial 2-torsion points, assumed rational here. Σ_J ≅ P^1_k is the quotient E/{±1}. The map ε_n is the 'leading coefficient' (symbol) map to tensor powers of t_E. On the previous page Grothendieck chose δ ∈ t_E, p ∈ F_2 with ε_2(p) = δ^2, and p' = θ_δ(p), the derivative of p along the invariant vector field δ. He showed that 1, p, …, p^n is a basis of F_{2n}^+ and that p' F_{2n-2}^+ = F_{2n+1}^-.

This page proves Proposition 1: the kernel of evaluation F_3 → k^J is F_3^- = k·p'.
- Step 1: an odd function f vanishes at every 2-torsion point x ≠ 0. Since x = -x, f(x) = -f(-x) = -f(x), so 2f(x) = 0 and f(x) = 0 because char ≠ 2. Hence the evaluation map kills F_3^-, and it suffices to show it is injective on F_3^+ = F_2.
- Step 2 (stronger Corollary): the 3×3 Vandermonde matrix (p(e_i)^α), for i ∈ J and 0 ≤ α ≤ 2, is invertible, i.e. the three values p(e_i) are pairwise distinct. Proof: p is even of degree 2, so it descends to a degree-1 function on Σ_J = P^1. Normalize coordinates so that the images of J are 0, 1, ∞. After an affine change (multiply by a nonzero scalar, add a constant), p(z) = 1/(z - t), where t is the image of the origin and t ∈ P^1 \ {0,1,∞} = U_{0,1}(k). Then p(0) = -1/t, p(1) = 1/(1-t) and p(∞) = 0 are distinct.

Next, p'^2 is even with a pole of order 6, so it lies in F_6^+ = span(1, p, p^2, p^3). Comparing leading symbols, ε_6(p'^2) = ε_6(p^3) = δ^6. This gives the Weierstrass relation (28): p'^2 = p^3 + a_1 p^2 + a_2 p + a_3, with the a_i uniquely determined. There is no p'-term because of the ± decomposition.

The next page identifies the cubic as ∏_{i∈J}(p - p(e_i)), using p'|J = 0 and the Vandermonde independence. It then normalizes a_1 = 0 (Σ p(e_i) = 0) in characteristic ≠ 3 to obtain the Weierstrass ℘.

Purpose: a coordinate-free, base-change-friendly derivation of the Legendre/Weierstrass presentation in characteristic ≠ 2. It is presumably meant for working over a base S and for moduli of elliptic curves with level-2 structure, which is where U_{0,1} = P^1 \ {0,1,∞} appears as the λ-line.
errors: Normalization issue: with the naive symbol maps, if p ~ z^{-2} then θ_δ p ~ -2 z^{-3}. This would give ε_3(p') = -2δ^3 and the classical relation p'^2 = 4p^3 + … . The claims ε_3(p') = δ^3 (previous page) and ε_6 p'^2 = ε_6 p^3 hold only if Grothendieck's ε_n carry compensating constants, or if the factor 4 has been silently dropped. The monic form on the next page, ∏(p - p(e_i)), inherits this.
The corollary's proof tacitly assumes the points of J are k-rational, so that they can be placed at 0, 1, ∞. Otherwise one argues after a separable extension, which is harmless.
Minor: the role of t is not stated explicitly; it is the image of the origin in Σ_J, which forces t ∉ {0,1,∞}.

ideas.what: Odd functions vanish at nontrivial 2-torsion points in char ≠ 2
Values of the degree-2 even function at the three 2-torsion points are distinct, proved via the quotient E/±1 ≅ P^1 with branch points normalized to 0, 1, ∞
ideas.modern_name: distinctness of the roots e_i of the Weierstrass cubic; Legendre λ-normalization
ideas.usually_credited_to: Weierstrass/Legendre (classical); algebraic version in Deligne's 'Courbes elliptiques: formulaire', Katz–Mazur

ideas.what: Derivation of the Weierstrass equation p'^2 = cubic in p via the ± decomposition of Riemann–Roch spaces

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful but entirely textbook derivation of the Weierstrass/Legendre equation for elliptic curves in characteristic ≠ 2. Its only distinctive feature is the intrinsic bookkeeping (symbol maps ε_n, derivation θ_δ, parity decomposition), which serves a moduli-of-elliptic-curves project but contains nothing new.
transcription_corrections: The page number '3' at top is a section/page marker, not part of the text.
'U_{0,1}(k)' denotes P^1 minus {0, 1, ∞}, consistent with the image.

In (28) the coefficients appear first written as g's/q's and then overwritten as a_1, a_2, a_3. The marginal note reads roughly 'a_1, a_2, a_3 ∈ k déterminés de façon unique (pas …)'; the final words are illegible, and 'distincts' is doubtful.
